title: Deadlocks, starvation and livelocks
description: Detect and prevent deadlocks, thread starvation, and livelocks in concurrent C# applications.

data.text: Concurrency problems are not always obvious from a code review. Deadlocks, starvation, and livelocks are failures of coordination that can freeze or degrade an application for minutes before anyone notices.

A deadlock occurs when two or more threads each hold a lock that the other needs, and neither can proceed. The classic conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. If any one of these is broken, a deadlock cannot occur.

data.title: Classic deadlock with two locks

data.text: A livelock looks like a deadlock but the threads are not blocked — they are actively running yet making no progress. This often happens when threads repeatedly detect a conflict and retry, but their retries always collide.

data.title: Livelock with aggressive retry

data.text: Thread starvation is a scheduling problem: low-priority threads never get enough CPU time because higher-priority threads monopolize the processor. In the ThreadPool, this can happen if long-running CPU-bound tasks continuously occupy threads.

items: **Avoid nested locks** — Acquire locks in a globally consistent order.
**Use timeouts** — `Monitor.TryEnter` with a timeout or `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync` with a timeout prevents indefinite waits.
**Prefer async I/O** — Frees threads instead of blocking them.
**Detect livelocks** — Add randomized backoff or jitter to retry logic.

data.title: ThreadPool starvation is silent
data.text: Unlike a deadlock, starvation does not freeze the application. It slows it down gradually. Monitor ThreadPool queue length and thread count with ETW or EventCounters to detect it early.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Deadlocks need four conditions; break any one to prevent them.
Livelocks waste CPU because threads keep retrying without progress.
Starvation slows an application when threads are chronically oversubscribed.
Use timeouts, consistent lock ordering, and async I/O to reduce risk.
